When the time for the fruit to ripen arrives, the fruits of suffering, pleasure, and so forth each manifest accordingly; therefore, various karmas arise from a mind that lacks intrinsic nature, just as the *karpāsa* seed later assumes the color of *khadira*.
If one holds this view— that there is a mind possessing intrinsic nature (svabhāva) which is called recollective cognition—
or if someone says that the life-principle (jīva) is also recollective cognition;
if one holds such views, then there would be no recollective mind nor a life-principle, for if they possessed intrinsic nature, there could be no forgetting.
If you claim that there is such a thing as forgetfulness, there are two faults:
first, if recollection has an intrinsic nature (svabhāva), then there can be no forgetfulness; if there is forgetfulness, then there can be no recollection.
Regarding such forgetfulness, does it possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or lack intrinsic nature?
If it possesses intrinsic nature, is it not contradictory to the nature of recollection?
If they are not contradictory, then within a single object, both the minds of recollection and forgetfulness should arise simultaneously at one and the same time.
If they were contradictory, there would be no forgetting in the absence of intrinsic nature (svabhāva); and if there is no recollection, what could possibly be forgotten?
If you claim that forgetting occurs because cognition arises first and then ceases, then in that case, intrinsic nature cannot be established.
If there is recollection and cognition, then intrinsic nature and instruments are useless, because recollection and cognition exist eternally.
If you say that [recollection] is established by means of instruments, then it would lack intrinsic nature, which entails a logical fault.
If the agent and the instrument were one and the same, there would be no recollection, because cognition would be eternally present.
If cognition were absent, the mind might at times be non-existent, which would mean it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If the mind exists at times, then there is no recollection or cognition.
If there is no recollection or cognition, the mind ought to have ceased.
If you claim that the mind is eternal because of the existence of some distinct entity, [that is not so].
At the time of direct realization, there should be no recollective cognition;
yet you claim that one uses direct realization as the basis for recollective cognition, and therefore the essence of recollective cognition is not lost.
This argument is incorrect.
Why is this? If a thing were eternally abiding, there could be no repeated practice (*abhyāsa*); it is only when things are of the same kind and similar that repeated practice is possible.
If there were no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the sense of similarity could be established.
If there were an intrinsic nature (svabhāva), one would necessarily always maintain a single object or a single phenomenon; therefore, there would be no resemblance.
Because there is no resemblance, there is no repeated practice (abhyāsa); because there is no repeated practice, there is no recollection or cognition.

If you establish that memory and cognition possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then inference and the other means of valid cognition would not be established, because they would be of a single essence.
Consequently, every state of doubt would have to be a definitive knowledge; desire would be the absence of desire; theft would be giving; and a wife would be one's mother.
If this cognition is not different from its own nature, does it exist prior [to the object] or does it exist posterior [to it]?
If it exists prior, since that which is to be cognized does not yet exist, what would the cognition cognize?
If it exists subsequently, then the principle that the effect exists within the cause is immediately subverted.
If you say it exists primordially, what is it that is perceived?
If you say that the "self" (ātman) is what is perceived—
This argument is not tenable, because the self cannot be apprehended by either of the two means of valid cognition: direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*).
If a thing exists, it must be apprehended by one of these two means of cognition.
For example, the five sense objects are so called because the cognition of the five sense faculties does not arise repeatedly; this is termed direct perception.
Inference (*anumāna*) consists in the arising of cognition based on what has been previously perceived.
First, consciousness arises; subsequently, one infers the existence of the sense faculty (*indriya*), because consciousness is never separate from its faculty.
It is like first seeing smoke and subsequently knowing that there is fire.

The self is not like that; it cannot be apprehended in the manner of form and other [sensory objects], because it transcends the domain of the sense faculties, nor can it be inferred in the manner of the sense faculties themselves.
Since there is no associated phenomenon (saṃprayukta-dharma) [to serve as a basis for inference], the self is not an object of cognition.
Therefore, if awakening were prior [to the object], it would not constitute awakening.
Thus, one knows that all phenomena are, in accordance with reality, devoid of intrinsic nature; their essential nature is solely true emptiness.

3. Chapter on Refuting Mahāyāna Views. Within the second section, "Refuting Adherence," of the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*, this is the third chapter, "Refuting Mahāyāna Views. Furthermore, it should be understood that this is for the purpose of refuting those among the students of Mahāyāna who harbor biased attachments.
If you say that all existence is due to conventional truth and all non-existence is due to ultimate truth,
then this question should be asked:
"O virtuous friend!..."
What is the ultimate truth?
What is the conventional truth?
The answer is:
All phenomena lack intrinsic nature; this is the ultimate truth.
To speak of an intrinsic nature within phenomena that lack intrinsic nature is called conventional truth, because it is a provisional designation of existence within what is non-existent.
Question:
This grasping has no intrinsic nature (svabhāva). Is it existent by virtue of relying on conventional discourse, or is it merely a matter of words?
If this grasping exists by relying on conventional discourse, then this grasping cannot be said [to exist].
Why is this? Because that which is grasped does not exist.
If this grasping were merely linguistic expression, then there would be nothing signified, because conventional language would not be established.
If it were the case that what is not established is conventional reality, this meaning would be untenable.

Furthermore, if you claim that grasping at intrinsic nature within that which lacks intrinsic nature is what constitutes the conventional, then how could that which is grasped as existing be non-existent?
Answer:

Because they belong to the category of perversion, one speaks of existence within non-existence; thus, even regarding phenomena such as impermanence, suffering, and non-self, one says that they all exist.
Virtues such as permanence and so forth do not exist in substance; they exist only as conventional designations.
To hold such a view is to be subsumed under the four inversions; therefore, although one grasps them as existing, they are in fact non-existent.
Question:
Are such inversions existent or non-existent?
If they are existent, then the claim that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature would be incorrect.
If [intrinsic nature] were non-existent, this adherence to perversion could not be established.
If it is claimed that adhering to the existence of intrinsic nature within that which lacks intrinsic nature constitutes conventional truth,
this argument is incorrect.
Why is this? Because the two truths cannot be said to exist, nor can they be said not to exist; they are neither existent nor non-existent.

As for the truth of ultimate reality (paramārtha-satya) being neither existent nor non-existent: it cannot be said to exist because there are no persons or phenomena, and it cannot be said not to exist because it reveals the two kinds of emptiness.

The conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is likewise: because it is of the nature of imagined construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), it cannot be said to exist; because it is of the nature of dependence on others (*paratantra-svabhāva*), it cannot be said to be non-existent.
Furthermore, in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there is no fixed existence of persons or dharmas; it is neither existent nor non-existent, and it is both empty and not non-empty.

The conventional truth is likewise: because it is of the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), it is not definitively non-existent; because it is of the nature of dependence on others (*paratantra-svabhāva*), it is not definitively existent.

Chapter Three: Revealing the Essence. Section One: The Chapter on the Three Causes. Furthermore, the essence of Buddha-nature is threefold; one should understand that its meaning is subsumed within the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
The three kinds refer to the so-called three causes and the three types of Buddha-nature.
As for the three causes: first, the cause of that which is to be attained; second, the cause of application; and third, the cause of perfection.

Regarding "that which should be attained" (*prāpya*): it is the *tathatā* manifested by the two kinds of emptiness. Because of this emptiness, one should attain the bodhicitta, the preparatory practices (*prayoga*), and so forth, up to the *dharmakāya* after the path; therefore, it is called "that which should be attained."

The causal condition of application refers to the bodhicitta; because of this mind, one is able to attain the factors conducive to enlightenment—the thirty-seven auxiliaries, the ten stages, and the ten perfections—as well as the dharmakāya after the attainment of the path. This is called the causal condition of application.
The perfection of the cause refers to the preparatory application (*prayoga*); through this application, one attains the perfection of the cause as well as the perfection of the fruit.
The perfection of the cause consists of the practices of merit and wisdom (*puṇya-jñāna-caryā*).
Regarding the perfection of the fruit, it refers to wisdom (*jñāna*), abandonment (*prahāṇa*), and beneficence (*anuśaṃsā*).

Among these three causes, the former consists essentially of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) suchness (*tathatā*), while the latter two consist essentially of conditioned aspiration and practice (*saṃskṛta-praṇidhāna-caryā*).
Regarding the three kinds of Buddha-nature, the causal stage that is to be attained inherently possesses these three natures:
first, the nature of abiding in its own essence; second, the nature of being drawn forth; and third, the nature of ultimate attainment.
The commentary states:
"Abiding in the nature of its own essence" refers to the stage of ordinary beings prior to the Path.
"Bringing forth the nature" extends from the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment upward, through to the final stage of the noble ones still in training (*śaikṣa*)."
The stage of attaining the nature (*prāpti-dharmatā*) refers to the level of the noble ones who have nothing more to learn (*aśaikṣa*).

Chapter Two: The Three Natures (*Tri-svabhāva*), from Part Three: The Section on Revealing the Essence of the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*. Furthermore, that which is subsumed under the three natures consists of the three non-natures (*tri-niḥsvabhāvatā*) and the three self-natures (*tri-svabhāva*).
The three natures of non-being are: first, the nature of signlessness; second, the nature of non-arising; and third, the nature of non-reality.
These three natures encompass the Tathāgata-nature exhaustively. Why is this so?
Because these three natures collectively constitute the essence [of reality], as for the nature of signlessness (*animitta-lakṣaṇatā*):
all phenomena are merely manifested through names and conventions; because their intrinsic nature lacks any defining characteristic, it is called the nature of signlessness.

Regarding the nature of non-arising: because all phenomena arise from causes and conditions, they do not arise through their own power, nor are they established by themselves or by both self and other; therefore, it is called the nature of non-arising.

Regarding "the absence of true nature": because all phenomena are devoid of a characteristic of truth, and because no other real nature can be found apart from them, it is called the absence of true reality.
Furthermore, regarding the three natures—first, the imagined (parikalpita); second, the dependent (paratantra);
and third, the perfected (pariniṣpanna)—one should know that there are ten meanings to be understood. What are these ten?

1. Differentiation of names; 2. accomplishment through conditions; 3. sustaining; 4. essential characteristics; 5. that which should be known; 6. explanation by way of causal matters; 7. reliance on objects; 8. thorough penetration; 9. the absence of [duality] and so forth; 10. basis.
Regarding the first, the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*): because it is provisionally designated in accordance with names and words, the nature of discrimination is established.

If these names and words did not exist, the nature of discrimination would not be established; therefore, one knows that this nature is merely manifested by names and words and lacks any real essence or characteristic. This is called the nature of discrimination.

The dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is the principle manifested by the twelve links of dependent origination; because it serves as the basis for the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), it is established as the dependent nature.

Regarding the nature of reality (*tathatā*): it is the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena and the object of the non-conceptual wisdom of the noble ones (*ārya*). It is established as the nature of reality for the sake of purifying the two natures, for the sake of liberation, or for the sake of eliciting all virtuous qualities; this is called the "discrimination of names."
Regarding the second point, establishment through conditions, a question is asked:
"By what causes and conditions does the nature of discrimination (parikalpita-svabhāva) manifest?
The answer is:
It manifests through the association of signs and names.
Question:
By what causes and conditions is the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) established?
Answer: It manifests by virtue of being conditioned by and grasping at the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Question:
On what basis is reality established?
The answer is:
it is manifested because the two natures—the imagined and the dependent—are utterly non-existent.
Therefore, it is called "conditioned arising.
Third, regarding "comprehensive maintenance," there are three natures and five categories of phenomena. As for the three natures, they are:
the imagined (parikalpita), the dependent (paratantra), and the perfected (pariniṣpanna).
The five dharmas are: first, marks; second, names; third, conceptual discrimination; fourth, noble wisdom; and fifth, suchness.
The first three are mundane wisdoms; noble wisdom is supramundane wisdom; and suchness is the unconditioned object.
In order to clarify that these five dharmas subsume the first three natures,
it is asked:
Among the five dharmas, how many dharmas subsume the first nature?
Answer: These five dharmas cannot be subsumed [within any category]. Why is this?
Because it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Question:
How many dharmas can subsume the second nature?
Answer: There are four dharmas that encompass it.
Question:
How many dharmas can encompass the third gender?
The answer is:
only the single dharma of suchness (tathatā) can encompass it.
Question:

If the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is subsumed by noble wisdom (āryajñāna), why is it said that the dependent nature is established through conditions based on the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva)? Answer:
The dependent nature is of two kinds: first, the defiled dependent nature; second, the pure dependent nature.
The defiled dependent nature is established by depending on conceptual discrimination;
the pure dependent nature is established by depending on suchness.
Regarding the four aspects of essence (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*), there are two types:
general (*sāmānya*) and specific (*viśeṣa*).

As for the general, because these three natures (*trisvabhāva*) universally enable the accomplishment of all other true realities—whether they be the two, three, four, or seven truths—the various true realities do not transcend the three natures; therefore, the three natures constitute the general essence of all true realities.
Regarding the second point, the distinct natures: within the three natures, each possesses its own substantial meaning.
What is this substantial meaning?
First, the nature of discrimination (parikalpita-svabhāva) is eternally non-existent; yet, this very fact constitutes its substantial reality within the context of the nature of discrimination.
Why is this? Because names and words are not erroneous.

Second, the essence of the dependent nature exists but is not real: it exists because of the confusion of consciousness regarding the faculties and their objects, yet it is not real because it is not suchness.
Why is this? Because the meaning of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) is non-erroneous.

Therefore, it is called "existent" in relation to the nature of conceptual differentiation (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), yet it is not truly existent in relation to the subsequent true nature (*tathatā*); thus, it is called "existence that is not real."
Third is the essence of true reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*): both existence and non-existence are true, because the essence of suchness (*tathatā*) is neither existent nor non-existent.
Question:
What is the true nature (*lakṣaṇa*) of these three natures?

Answer: Regarding the true characteristic of the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), it consists of the superimposition and denial of persons and phenomena; because one understands this nature, these attachments do not arise.
These persons and phenomena that constitute the characteristic of discrimination are merely products of discrimination.
If one observes according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), that these persons and phenomena exist is called the "clinging to exaggeration" (*samāropa-grāha*).
If one observes according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), that these persons and phenomena do not exist is called the "clinging to deprecation" (*apavāda-grāha*).

If one thoroughly penetrates this nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), then the two attachments of superimposition (*samāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*) will not arise; this is called the characteristic of the true nature of discrimination.

Furthermore, regarding the characteristic of the true nature of the dependent (*paratantra-svabhāva*): because one understands this nature, the superimposition and denial of the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*) do not arise; this is called the characteristic of the dependent nature.
Regarding this grasper and the grasped: if one views them as truly existent, this is an exaggeration and is called the view of eternalism.
If one views them as definitively non-existent on the conventional level, this is a deprecation and is called the view of nihilism.
If one penetrates these two natures, the dual attachments to annihilation and permanence will both fail to arise; this is called the characteristic of the true nature of the dependent.

Because there is only consciousness appearing as objects, there is neither subject nor object; because there is no subject or object, there is no attachment to superimposition (samāropa); and because there is consciousness appearing as objects, there is no attachment to denial (apavāda).

Furthermore, regarding the characteristics of true reality (*tathatā*): through the understanding of this nature, the attachments to existence, non-existence, and the superimposition or denial [of qualities] cannot arise. Why is this so?
If one clings to emptiness as being existent, it is called the slander of superimposition (*samāropa*).
If one clings to emptiness as being non-existent, it is called the slander of denial (*apavāda*).
If one thoroughly penetrates this nature, these two types of clinging do not arise; this is called the characteristic of true reality (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "the five should be known," etc., it is asked: Of these three natures, how many should be known and how many should not be known?
It is answered:
All should be known. Why is this?
Because by knowing the three natures, one can penetrate the three gates of liberation and eliminate the three obstacles.
Knowing the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), one can penetrate the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*) and eliminate the afflictions of the flesh.
Knowing the nature of dependence on others (*paratantra-svabhāva*), one penetrates the gate of liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*) and eliminates the afflictions of the skin.
Knowing true reality, one is able to penetrate the gate of liberation that is signless and eliminate the afflictions of the mind.
This is because there is first the obstacle to liberation, next the obstacle to meditative concentration, and finally the obstacle to omniscience.
Question:
Among the three natures, how many natures are indestructible,
and how many natures are destructible?
The answer is:
two natures cannot be extinguished, while one nature can be extinguished. Why is this?
The nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is originally non-existent, and therefore it cannot be extinguished.
The nature of ultimate reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is originally true, and therefore it cannot be extinguished.
Although the nature of dependence on others (*paratantra-svabhāva*) exists, it is not real; therefore, it can be extinguished.
For this reason, it is said that one "should know" and so forth.
This is explained by way of six causes. The Buddhas' teaching of the Dharma is of two kinds:
first, sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*); second, sūtras of non-definitive meaning (*neyārtha*).
Regarding the sūtras of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*): it is by means of these three natures that the Buddha taught the sūtras of provisional meaning.
It is like when one knows that an object exists in the darkness because of a lamp; later, by means of the lamp, one is able to clearly perceive the object that was previously in the darkness.
The Tathāgata is likewise: because there are those who cling to the three natures, he teaches the sūtras of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).
For those who have realized the three natures, [the truth] is naturally manifest; these are called the sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"If a person has attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), they do not fall back.
Question:
How is this statement established?
The answer is:
it is established by virtue of the existence of the three natures (trisvabhāva).

The Tathāgata, with reference to the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), speaks of the patience regarding the primordial non-arising; with reference to the nature of dependence on others (*paratantra-svabhāva*), he speaks of the patience regarding the non-arising of intrinsic nature; and with reference to the nature of reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), he speaks of the patience regarding the primordial non-arising of the fundamental nature of afflictions, defilements, and suffering.
Question:
Based on what nature does the Tathāgata speak this meaning,
saying that all dharmas are without arising and without cessation, originally quiescent, and by nature in nirvāṇa?
Answer: These words are spoken in reference to the nature of signlessness (*animitta*). Question:
Based on what dharma does the Tathāgata say that all dharmas are like illusions? Answer:
He speaks based on the nature of non-arising.
Question: Based on what dharma did the Tathāgata speak these words:
"All dharmas are like space"?
Answer: This is explained in terms of the nature of ultimate reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Therefore, because the Buddha taught based on the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), there are sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and sūtras of non-definitive meaning (*neyārtha*).
Regarding the seventh point, the objects of reliance:
it is asked, "To what objects of knowledge do these three natures correspond?
It is answered:
The nature of discrimination is exclusively the object of the delusions of ordinary beings, not the object of noble wisdom.
Why is this? Because it lacks intrinsic substance and characteristics.
The dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is the object of the conventional wisdom of both the noble ones and ordinary beings, because it exists conventionally.
The perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) is exclusively the object of the non-conceptual wisdom of the noble ones, because it accords with reality as it is and as it ought to be.
"According to measure, it encompasses all; according to principle, it is free from inversion—this is called relying on the object.
Regarding the eight types of penetration, a question is asked:

If a practitioner of meditation penetrates the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), should it be said that they are practicing within the characteristics of grasping at signs, or should it be said that they are not practicing within the characteristics of grasping at signs?"
Answer: If one discriminates by means of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), it can be said that one acts within the characteristics of grasping;
if one penetrates [reality] by means of supramundane non-conceptual knowledge (*lokottara-nirvikalpa-jñāna*), it can be said that one does not act within the characteristics of grasping.
Therefore, the dependent nature and the imagined nature are both equally without marks (*animitta*).
Just as the imagined is [without marks] in relation to the dependent, so too is the perfected nature.
Question:
When a practitioner of meditation is able to enter the nature of discrimination (parikalpita-svabhāva) according to the principle of reality, what nature do they illuminate and comprehend?
The answer is:
they comprehend the nature of reality (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).
Question:
When a practitioner of meditation enters true nature according to the principle of reality, what nature do they illuminate and realize? Answer:

Because one realizes the nature of dependence (*paratantra-svabhāva*), one subsequently attains the nature of reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*); this is called "penetrative realization" (*prativedha*).
Ninth, regarding the phrase "if there were no [imagined nature]," the question is asked:
If the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) does not exist, what fault would there be?
Answer:

If the nature of non-discrimination did not exist, then names and conventions could not be established; because names and conventions would not be established, the dependent nature could not be accomplished, and even the categories of the pure and the impure would all fail to be established.
Question: If the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) does not exist, what fault would there be? Answer:
If the dependent nature did not exist, all afflictions would be extinguished spontaneously without the need for effort.
If that were the case, the category of purity could not be established either.
[The opponent] asks:
If true reality (*tathatā*) did not exist, what fault would there be?
The answer is:
if true reality did not exist, then the object of purification in all its aspects (*sarvākāra-viśuddha-viṣaya*) could not be established.
"All" (sarva) refers to the exhaustive inclusion of both the ultimate and the conventional truths individually;
"all aspects" (sarvākāra) refers to their comprehensive inclusion as a whole. Question:
Regarding this true nature (tathatā), can it be established as pure or established as impure?
The answer is:
it cannot be definitively described as either pure or impure.
If concentration were inherently pure, then all sentient beings would attain liberation effortlessly without the need for cultivation.
If concentration were inherently impure, then all sentient beings would find no fruit or reward from practicing the Path.
If concentration were definitively pure, then there would be no dharmas of ordinary beings;
if concentration were definitively impure, then there would be no dharmas of noble ones. Why is this so?
Since both the pure and the impure categories take suchness as their basis:
if it were definitively pure, it would not be ignorance;
if it were impure, it would not be prajñā.
In these two states, the nature is not different; therefore, this true suchness (tathatā) is neither pure nor impure.

Why is this? It is because one wishes to demonstrate that true suchness is distinct from the various sense faculties, such as the eye, and distinct from the mind of meditative concentration and so forth.
Regarding the various faculties such as the eye and so forth: since these faculties are not defiled, they should likewise attain purity identical to that of the principle of reality (*tathatā*).
However, this is not the case; because they have out-flowing karma (*sāsrava-karma*) as their cause, they are fundamentally impure.

True Suchness (tathatā) is not so; abiding in the stage of Buddhahood, its original nature is pure, and there is no sense of it being impure from the beginning; therefore, it differs from the various faculties.

As for its difference from the concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*) and so forth: the essence of concentration is inherently pure by nature and could thus accord with True Suchness, yet because it is consumed by the four afflictions, it becomes transformed into something impure.
If the principle of *tathatā* (suchness) were inherently pure in this manner, it would not be so; for even while remaining within the shell of ignorance, it is ultimately never defiled by it.
Question: Among these three natures (*trisvabhāva*), how many lack substantiality yet are capable of producing that which possesses substantiality?
Answer: It is only the discrimination of the non-substantiality of the single nature that can produce the substance of the dependent nature.
Question:
Among these, how many natures possess substantial existence and are capable of producing that which possesses substantial existence?
The answer is:

only the nature of the *paratantra* (the dependent) exists as a non-substantial entity, yet it is still able to produce the substance of the *paratantra*, just as ignorance produces the various formations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth.
Question:
Among these three natures, how many possess substantial existence (*dravyasat*), and which can produce that which lacks substantial existence? Answer:
Because the true single nature can extinguish the dependent nature, rendering it without substance, this is called "if there were none," and so forth.
Regarding the ten bases, a question is asked:
upon what dharma does the imagined nature depend to be established?
Answer: It is established by means of three factors.
What are these three?
First, the characteristic; second, the name; third, the mental construction.
Based upon these three, the nature of discrimination (parikalpita-svabhāva) is established. Question:
Upon what does the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) depend for its establishment?
The answer is:
it is established by means of four factors.
The four dharmas refer to characteristics (*nimitta*), names (*nāman*), conceptualization (*vikalpa*), and noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).
Based on these four dharmas, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is established. Question:
Upon what phenomena is suchness established?
The answer is:
this nature is without abiding and without attachment; it has no locus of dependence, and its object is non-conceptual.

3. The Tathāgatagarbha Section. Within the third part, "The Exposition of the Essence," of the *Buddhadhātuśāstra*, namely the third section, "The Tathāgatagarbha Section": Furthermore, it should be known that there are three meanings of the tathāgatagarbha.
What are the three?
First, the treasury of that which is subsumed; second, the treasury of concealment; and third, the treasury of the capacity to subsume.
Regarding the first, the treasury of what is subsumed: the Buddha taught that, with reference to the suchness (*tathatā*) of intrinsic nature, all sentient beings are the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Regarding the term "Tathā" (Thus), there are two meanings:
first, Tathatā-jñāna (the wisdom of suchness); second, Tathatā-viṣaya (the object of suchness). Because both are non-erroneous, they are called "Tathatā.
Regarding the term "Āgata" (Come), it refers to coming from one's own nature and arriving at the attainment [of that nature]; thus, he is named Tathāgata (Thus-Come One).
Therefore, although the nature of the Tathāgata is designated by the name "cause," it should also receive the name "fruit.

Upon reaching the realization that its essence is non-dual, there is only a distinction based on clarity and turbidity: while in the causal stage, because it opposes the two kinds of emptiness, ignorance arises and it becomes intermingled with afflictions; thus, it is called "defiled and turbid."
Although it is not yet manifest, it will certainly become so; therefore, it is called "to be attained.
When one reaches the stage of fruition, it merges with the two kinds of emptiness; being free from further afflictive entanglements and untainted by defilements, it is called "pure."
Because the fruit has already manifested, it is called "attainment" (prāpti).
For example, the nature of water is neither inherently clear nor turbid; it is only due to being defiled or undefiled that it receives the names "clear" or "turbid."

If water is turbid and disturbed by silt and dregs, it is not clear; yet, though it is not clear, its inherent nature as water does not lose its clarity. If one employs skillful means to settle the sediment, it then attains purity. Thus we know that the designations "pure" and "impure" are obtained based on the presence or absence of defilement; they do not pertain to the water-nature itself possessing inherent purity or impurity, which would otherwise lead to such a conclusion.

The two kinds of Buddha-nature are likewise thus: they are identical in their single true suchness (tathatā) and possess no distinct substance; however, because they contradict the principle of emptiness, deluded attachments arise, and because they are defiled and disturbed by afflictions (kleśa), they are termed "turbid."

If one does not contradict the two emptinesses and the single characteristic of suchness, then ignorance will not arise and one will not be defiled by afflictions; for this reason, it is provisionally designated as "pure.

As for what is called the "treasury" (garbha), all sentient beings are entirely within the wisdom of the Tathāgata, and thus it is named a treasury; this is because the wisdom of suchness accords with the realm of suchness.

All sentient beings are certainly none who transcend the realm of suchness (tathatā), for they are all sustained by the Tathāgata; therefore, these sentient beings who are thus contained are called the "Tathāgatagarbha" (the womb/embryo of the Tathāgata).
Furthermore, there are three kinds of "treasuries":
First, the incomparability of manifesting the correct object; for apart from the realm of suchness (*tathatā*), there is no other distinct realm that transcends this realm.
Second, the incomparability of manifesting correct practice; for outside of this wisdom, there is no other superior wisdom that surpasses it.
Third, it is called "incomparable" because it manifests the supreme fruit, as there is no other fruit that surpasses this one;
hence it is called "incomparable.
Because this fruit can encompass and conceal all sentient beings, sentient beings are said to be the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Second, regarding "concealment as the treasury": the Tathāgata himself remains hidden and does not manifest, and for this reason it is called a "treasury.
As for the term "Tathāgata," there are two meanings:

first, it signifies being "thus" (tathā) without inversion. Because of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), one is said to be inverted; because one is free from false conceptualization, it is termed "thus" (*tathā*).

Second is the meaning of manifesting eternal abiding: this refers to how Suchness, proceeding from its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*) to its attainment (*prāpti*), remains without change in its essence; therefore, it has the meaning of being eternal.
When the *tathāgatagarbha* abides prior to the path, it is obscured by afflictions (*kleśa*) and thus not seen by sentient beings; for this reason, it is called a "womb" (*garbha*).

Third, it is called a "womb" because it can encompass [all virtues]: when one abides in the stage of the *tathāgata-yogyatā-garbha*, all the merits exceeding the sands of the Ganges at the stage of fruition are already fully encompassed therein.
If it were only at the time of attaining the fruit that this nature were said to be acquired, then this nature would be impermanent.
Why? Because it is not something newly acquired.
Therefore, one knows it exists inherently; for this reason, it is called "eternal.

**Chapter Four: Distinguishing the Characteristics (Lakṣaṇavibhāga)** **Section One: The Nature of the Self-Substance (Svabhāvalakṣaṇavarga)** Furthermore, it should be understood that the Buddha-nature, in its aspect as all-encompassing seeds (*sarvabījaka*), possesses ten meanings.

Regarding the ten characteristics: first, the characteristic of intrinsic nature; second, the characteristic of cause; third, the characteristic of fruit; fourth, the characteristic of functional capacity; fifth, the characteristic of comprehensive inclusion; sixth, the characteristic of differentiation; seventh, the characteristic of stages; eighth, the characteristic of pervasiveness; ninth, the characteristic of immutability; and tenth, the characteristic of non-differentiation.
Regarding the first, the characteristic of its own essence (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*), there are two kinds:
first, specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); second, general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
There are three types of specific characteristics.
What are these three?
First, the nature of wish-fulfilling merit; second, the nature of non-differentiation; and third, the nature of lubricity.
Regarding the characteristic of wish-fulfilling merit, it refers to the fivefold qualities of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
What are the five?
First, the self-nature of the *tathāgatagarbha* is the meaning of "garbha.
Because all phenomena do not transcend the self-nature of the *tathāgata*, and because their characteristic is non-self (*anātman*), all phenomena are said to be the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Second is the treasury of the True Dharma (saddharmapiṭaka). It is called a "treasury" in the sense of being a cause.

Because all the true dharmas of the noble ones, such as the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), take this nature as their object, causing those not yet arisen to arise and those already arisen to reach fulfillment, it is therefore called the treasury of the True Dharma.
Third is the *dharmakāya-garbha*; "attainment" (*prāpti*) is the meaning of "garbha" (*garbha*).

All noble ones (*ārya*) have faith and delight in the true nature (*samyaktva*), and they have faith and delight in the aspiration to hear it. Because of this mind of faith and delight, it causes all noble ones to attain the four virtues as well as all the Tathāgata’s merits, which exceed the sands of the Ganges. Therefore, this nature is called the *dharmakāya-garbha*.
The fourth is the supramundane treasury (*lokottara-garbha*); "treasury" here carries the sense of "reality.
There are three faults in the world:
first, because it can be extinguished through its antidotes, it is called "mundane"; this Dharma, however, has no antidote and is therefore called "supramundane."

The second is called "mundane" because it does not abide in stillness; since the retribution of the deluded mind perishes moment by moment and does not remain, this dharma is not like that and is therefore called "supramundane."

Third, because of the presence of inverted views, the mind remains in the world in a state of constant inversion; just as when one is within the three realms, one can by no means perceive the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) within the mind. Because it is false and illusory, it is called "the world" (*loka*).
Because this Dharma can transcend the mundane world, it is called "the true reality" (tattva) and serves as the treasury for transcending the world.
Fifth is the "treasury of natural purity," where "treasury" (garbha) carries the sense of being secret.
If all phenomena accord with this nature, they are termed "internal"; being correct and not deviant, they are pure.
If phenomena oppose this principle, they are termed "external"; being deviant and not correct, they are called defiled and turbid.
Therefore, it is called the naturally pure treasury (*prakṛti-viśuddha-garbha*).
Thus, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* says:
"World-Honored One!"
Buddha-nature is the Tathāgatagarbha, the treasury of the True Dharma, the treasury of the Dharmakāya, the supramundane treasury, and the treasury of intrinsic purity.
Because these five treasuries (pañcakośa) are explained, the qualities of the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) are manifested.
To clarify this meaning, the Buddha spoke of the wish-fulfilling jewel.

For example, just as a person, by virtue of past karma, obtains a wish-fulfilling jewel, and once they have obtained it, whatever matters they desire are spontaneously accomplished according to their will.

The Buddha-nature is likewise; by serving spiritual friends, cultivating various merits and wisdom, and thereby eliciting this nature, it accords with the intentions of the practitioner, such that each individually attains the fruit of the three vehicles.
The wish-fulfilling merit is its specific characteristic.

Regarding the non-dual nature of these two: for ordinary beings, noble ones, and all Buddhas, the mind-nature is free from the faults of discrimination; it is the state of ultimate purity of merit, pervading all equally like space.

Furthermore, it is like earthenware, silver, and golden vessels: although these three differ from one another, their essential nature is equally empty. Because there is no distinction within that emptiness, they are said to possess a non-differentiated nature.
The commentary states:
"Faults" refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*);
"virtues" refers to noble ones in training (*śaikṣa*).
Those who are ultimately pure are the Buddhas.
Although these three locations differ, their nature is not distinct.
Here, the earth is used as a metaphor for ordinary beings, silver for those in training, and gold for the Buddhas.
Although the three vessels differ, their emptiness is of one kind.
Furthermore, they possess the three meanings of existence, purity, and pervasiveness.
"Existence" manifests the meaning of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); "purity" manifests the meaning of being unstained; and "pervasiveness" manifests the meaning of being unobstructed.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“The realm of sentient beings is not different from the Dharma-body, and the Dharma-body is not different from the realm of sentient beings.
For this reason, they are non-dual and without distinction; there is only a difference in name.”

Thus, the Buddha-nature is equally and universally pervasive throughout these three stages; because it undergoes no transformation due to the categories of purity and impurity, it is said to be like the nature of space.
Third, regarding "lubricity," this explains the nature of the Tathāgata.
It manifests the meaning of cause and effect among sentient beings, because it has the characteristic of being soft and supple toward sentient beings through great compassion.
Great Compassion has three meanings: first, essence;
second, greatness; and third, distinctness.
Regarding the meaning of essence, it takes prajñā as its essence.
Prajñā is twofold:
first, non-conceptual true wisdom; second, conceptual conventional wisdom.
Here, we take conceptual wisdom as the essence of great compassion (mahākaruṇā), because great compassion arises by taking sentient beings as its object.
Regarding the two great meanings, there are five aspects:
first, as provisions; second, as characteristics; third, as the sphere of practice; fourth, as equality; and fifth, as the ultimate.
First, as for "provision" (*sambhāra*): it is because it can serve as the twofold provision for the practices of great merit and wisdom.
Second, as for "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*): it is because it can observe sentient beings suffering from the three types of suffering and deliver them all.
Third, as for being the sphere of practice, it is because all sentient beings of the three realms are taken as its object.
Fourth, as for being impartial, it is because one gives rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.
Regarding the five "most extreme" qualities, they are so called because there is no further practice superior to these once they have been cultivated.
Regarding the meaning of the three "distinctive" aspects, there are eight types:

first, the distinction of intrinsic nature; the immeasurable compassion (*karuṇā*) has non-hatred (*adveṣa*) as its nature, while great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) has non-delusion (*amoha*) as its nature.

Second is the distinction of their characteristics: for ordinary compassion (*karuṇā*), the characteristic is the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); for great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), the characteristic is the three types of suffering.
Third is the distinction of their spheres of activity: for ordinary compassion, the sphere is the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); for great compassion, the sphere extends throughout all three realms.

Fourth is the distinction of stage (*bhūmi*): for ordinary compassion (*karuṇā*), the fourth dhyāna constitutes its stage; for great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), the untainted fruit of a Tathāgata constitutes its stage.

Fifth is the distinction of object (*viṣaya*): for ordinary compassion, ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles constitute its objects; for great compassion, only bodhisattvas and Buddhas constitute its objects.

Sixth is the distinction of qualities: one who possesses compassion (*karuṇā*) has the quality of being free from desire for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), whereas one who possesses great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) has the quality of being free from desire for all three realms.

Seventh is the distinction of rescue and relief: one who possesses compassion has only the intention to uproot suffering, but lacks the actual act of uprooting it; one who possesses great compassion has both the intention and the act.

Eighth is the distinction between ultimate and non-ultimate: one who possesses compassion can provide a minor, temporary relief but cannot provide genuine salvation, whereas one who possesses great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) can provide eternal salvation because they never abandon sentient beings.
"Moistening" (snigdha) signifies its capacity for cohesion; "smoothness" (ślakṣṇa) signifies its tendency to turn away from faults and toward virtues.
For example, the water element also possesses two capacities:
first, it can cohere scattered objects, precisely because it is smooth and not rough.

Because of moisture, there is cohesion; because of smoothness, there is no roughness. Thus, moisture is the cause and smoothness is the effect; this is what is called the principle of manifest cause and effect.

Furthermore, regarding the meaning that intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) is its universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*): it is as in the previous analogies of true emptiness, the water element, and so forth, for in all these cases, intrinsic purity constitutes their universal characteristic.

Because the Tathāgata-nature remains undefiled within the afflictions; because these four characteristics serve as obstacles to the four delusions; because they are not attainable by the [first] four types of persons; because they serve as the basis for the four virtues; because they bring about the departure from the four inversions; and because they act as the antidote that extinguishes birth and death—therefore, it is said that the four characteristics are one in their commonality yet distinct in their threefold differentiation.
The single common characteristic is solely the characteristic of intrinsic purity.
The three distinct characteristics are: first, the inconceivable; second, that which is to be attained; and third, immeasurable merit.
This is called the characteristic of its own essence (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*).

Chapter 4: Discerning Characteristics, Part 2: Clarifying the Causes, Section 2. Furthermore, one should know that there are four kinds of causes which can remove four obstructions and realize the meaning of the Tathāgata-nature.
The four causes are: first, faith and delight in the Mahāyāna; second, non-conceptual prajñā; third, the space-penetrating samādhi; and fourth, the great compassion of a bodhisattva.

The four obstacles are: first, aversion to and rejection of the Mahāyāna; second, the clinging adherence to the view of a self-body (satkāya-dṛṣṭi); third, fear of birth and death; and fourth, a lack of delight in observing activities that benefit others.
First, it obstructs the icchantikas; second, it obstructs non-Buddhists; third, it obstructs śrāvakas; and fourth, it obstructs pratyekabuddhas.
Due to these four delusions, these four types of persons are unable to perceive the dharmakāya of intrinsic purity.
Briefly stated, there are three types of sentient beings in the world:

first, those who delight in birth and death and constantly exist therein; second, those who delight in the cessation of birth and death; and third, those who delight in neither, remaining in a state where both existence and its cessation are equally forgotten.
Those who delight in birth-and-death and existence are further divided into two types:
first, those who loathe and turn their backs on the path of liberation, who lack the nature for *nirvāṇa*, and who resolutely delight in birth-and-death while taking no pleasure in *nirvāṇa*.
Second, those who have already fallen into a fixed position.

Regarding this "fixed position": they are neither noble nor ordinary; they neither advance nor retreat, and have nothing to grasp. Yet, while being insiders within the Buddha-dharma, they turn their backs on the Mahāyāna.
For the sake of such a person, the Buddha spoke these words:
"I am not his teacher, nor is he my disciple. Śāriputra!
This person enters from light darkness into heavy darkness, and further from heavy darkness into blinding darkness.
Taking darkness as a friend, they further take icchantikas as a friend; for this reason, I say that this person has these two kinds of pleasure.
Regarding those who extinguish the existence of birth and death, there are two types:
first, those who fall into what is not a skillful means; second, those who fall into [a limited] skillful means.
Within the category of falling into what is not a skillful means, there are further two types:
First are the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), numbering ninety-six kinds.

Second are those within the Buddha-dharma who hold views identical to the non-Buddhists; because they give rise to false attachments and the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) regarding the True Dharma, they are unable to fully comprehend the meaning of the authentic teachings.
For this reason, the Buddha spoke these words:
"If one does not believe in and delight in true emptiness, then one is no different from the non-Buddhists.
Furthermore, there are those with overweening pride who grasp at emptiness as a mere view; yet this true emptiness is, in fact, the gate of liberation.
Based on this gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*), one gives rise to an attachment to emptiness, asserting that all things, whether existent or non-existent, are equally empty.

This attachment to emptiness is itself a state of nothingness; because it is nothingness, the principles of both cause and effect and the two truths are lost. By clinging to this fault of emptiness, one falls into false nihilism (*mithyā-uccheda*).
These types of attachments arise from emptiness and therefore constitute false attachments.
Since no false attachment fails to be extinguished by means of emptiness, this particular attachment—having arisen in dependence upon emptiness itself—cannot be cured.
For this reason, the Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
"If a person gives rise to the grasping of the view of self as large as Mount Sumeru, I would still permit it. Why is this?"
Because it is subject to cessation,
if this person of overweening pride were to give rise to even a quarter of a hair-tip’s worth of attachment to emptiness, I would urgently rebuke him and absolutely not permit it.
Regarding the two types of practitioners who fall into the preparatory stage (*upāya*), there are two:
first, the *śrāvaka*, who practices for his own benefit and seeks only his own liberation without acting for the sake of others;
second, the *pratyekabuddha*, who takes no pleasure in nor engages in altruism, but merely gives rise to a mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
"Those who lack joy" do not delight in benefiting others.
"Those who lack activity" understand that they have no business of saving others, acting solely for the sake of their own awakening and self-benefit.

Because they give rise only to a mind of equanimity—where this equanimity is a mind abiding in impartiality, neither wishing to benefit others nor intending to harm them—they awaken by themselves alone; hence they are called Pratyekabuddhas (Solitary Realizers).
It is the same for those śrāvakas who have fallen into the stage of expedient means.

For example, when the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, the two bhikṣus Madhyantika and Aśvajit did not go; it was only later, when Kāśyapa convened the collection of the Dharma-piṭaka, that they were summoned and finally emerged.
Kāśyapa rebuked him, saying:
"Did you attain the noble path under the Buddha?
He replied, "Indeed I did."
Furthermore, he rebuked him, saying:
"You have committed a great transgression. Although you shall now depart, I entrust the Buddha-dharma to you to uphold.
If you do not act in accordance with the Dharma, the fault and loss shall belong to you."
That person gladly accepts the confession and receives the instructions to practice accordingly.

As for those who find joy in neither [of the two], this refers to those of the sharpest faculties who practice the Mahāyāna; they do not share the icchantikas' delight in birth-and-death (saṃsāra), nor do they fall into the lack of skillful means by adhering like the non-Buddhists (tīrthika), nor do they fall into the realm of skillful means as do those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).

Therefore, this person fully practices the path of the equality of birth-and-death and nirvana; dwelling in non-dwelling, though they course through birth-and-death, they are not defiled by it, and though they course through nirvana, they do not regard it as pure. Yet, out of great compassion, they do not abandon birth-and-death, and out of prajñā, they do not abandon nirvana.
"Not departing from nirvana" distinguishes [this teaching] from the attachment of the śrāvakas who abide eternally in the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
"Not abandoning saṃsāra" distinguishes it from the icchantikas who take pleasure in saṃsāra.
Those who delight in and are attached to birth and death are called icchantikas.
Those within the Buddha-dharma who have fallen into fixed determination are likewise icchantikas.
These two types of persons fall into the category of those fixed in wrongness (mithyātva-niyata-rāśi).
If one delights in the cessation of birth-and-death and existence, that person falls into what is not a skillful means and thus belongs to the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*).
If a person delights in the cessation of birth-and-death and existence, they fall into skillful means; this also applies to those who delight in neither.
Those who have attained the former two [stages] cultivate the path of equality; such persons are within the assembly of those fixed in rightness (*samyaktva-niyāma*).

Apart from those who have left behind the practice of the Mahāyāna and are cultivating the path of unobstructed realization, the remaining four types of persons—*icchantikas*, non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), *śrāvakas*, and *pratyekabuddhas*—do not see the Buddha-nature because they possess four kinds of obstructions.
What are the four obstructions?
First is the obstruction of the icchantika, which consists of reviling and turning one's back on the Mahāyāna.
To remedy this, the Buddha taught that bodhisattvas should cultivate faith and delight in the Dharma of the Mahāyāna.
Second, giving rise to the grasping of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) regarding all phenomena is an obstacle for non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
To counteract this, the Buddha taught that bodhisattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Third, to have a fixed attachment to the perception of suffering and a mind of aversion and fear within the cycle of birth and death is an obstacle for Śrāvakas.
To counteract this, the Buddha taught that Bodhisattvas practice the samādhi of the shattering of emptiness (prabheda-śūnyatā-samādhi).

Regarding the samādhi of emptiness: from the first bhūmi upward, one is able to attain this samādhi, whereby one breaks through attachments such as that to empty space. At the time of entering contemplation, one neither identifies with existence or non-existence nor departs from existence or non-existence; it is analogous to the simultaneous contemplation of the ultimate and the conventional in the eighth bhūmi.

As for what distinguishes it from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*): from the eighth stage upward, there is no entering or emerging from meditative absorption; thus, while the entry into the first stage is the same [as the eighth], the emergence from it is different.
To turn one's back on the welfare of sentient beings and to form the intention of abandoning them constitutes an obstacle to the Pratyekabuddha.
To counteract this, the Buddha taught the cultivation of the great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) of a bodhisattva.
The great compassion of a bodhisattva has the welfare of others as its primary activity.
It is clarified that the pratyekabuddha contemplates only his own causes and conditions and lacks the intention to deliver others; therefore, he possesses no great compassion.
It is the same for the śrāvakas.

In order to extinguish these four obstacles, they take the four factors—faith, aspiration, and so forth—as causes, causing the bodhisattvas to cultivate these causes so as to attain the supreme purity of the dharma-body; this is called the pure cause of buddha-nature.
Such a person is named a son of the Buddha; therefore, there are four meanings of being a son of the Buddha:
first, cause; second, condition; third, reliance; and fourth, accomplishment.
Regarding the initial mention of "causes," there are two:
first, Buddha-nature; second, faith and aspiration.
Of these two dharmas, Buddha-nature is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), while faith and aspiration are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

Faith and aspiration, in terms of their intrinsic nature, constitute the *vidyā-hetu* (revealing cause) for attaining Buddhahood, because they are able to manifest the nature of the *nidāna-hetu* (causal basis).
Faith and aspiration, in terms of their applied practice, constitute the *janaka-hetu* (generating cause), because they are able to give rise to all [virtuous] practices.

Second, regarding the conditions (*pratyaya*): it refers to the *prajñāpāramitā*, which can give birth to the body of a bodhisattva, because it serves as the condition for the family of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) merit.
Third, regarding the support (*niśraya*): it refers to the meditative concentrations on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) and so forth.
Those who possess the view of existence cling to nihilism, for they hold that there is no basis for the existence of pleasure, purity, and so forth.
The Bodhisattva cultivates the samādhi of the shattering of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vibheda-samādhi*), which is able to eliminate that clinging.
By the power of this concentration, the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-body becomes firm and solid, rather than weak and frail.
Regarding the fourfold accomplishment: because the Bodhisattva’s great compassion and activities for the benefit of others are inexhaustible.

Since True Suchness is inexhaustible and sentient beings are infinite, the activities for their benefit are likewise inexhaustible; this is because the Buddha-nature serves as the cause for those who are to attain it.

First, the cause is like the father’s body; second, the conditions are like the mother; third, the basis is like the womb; and fourth, the accomplishment is like the nurse. For these four reasons, all bodhisattvas are called "sons of the Buddha."

3. Chapter on Manifesting the Fruits: Section Four, Distinguishing Characteristics, Part Three, Manifesting the Fruits. Furthermore, the meaning of the characteristics of the fruits should be understood.
Regarding the characteristics of the fruits, there are two stages:
first, the two positions of ordinary beings and sages prior to the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*), in which the four virtues are not attained.

Second, regarding the various stages of the ten bhūmis: prior to these stages, the four virtues such as faith and aspiration serve as the cause for the pure Buddha-nature and act as the remedy for the four inversions.
It should be understood that the four marks, the merits, and the *pāramitās* of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body are its fruit. Regarding the four inversions (*catur-viparyāsa*):

to perceive permanence in the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), such as form (*rūpa*), which are in reality impermanent; to perceive pleasure in what is in reality suffering; to perceive a self in what is in reality selfless; and to perceive purity in what is in reality impure—these are called the four inversions.
There are three meanings of "perversion" (*viparyāsa*):
first, that which is destroyed by insight (*darśana-heya*); second, that which is destroyed by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*); and third, that which is destroyed by neither.

When one perceives the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one can eliminate the perversion of views; when meditative concentration definitively breaks the afflictions of deliberation (*vicikitsā-āsrava*), one can eliminate the perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*); and that which is destroyed by neither eliminates the perversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*).
To counteract these four [misconceptions], the four non-erroneous [realizations] are taught. What are the four?
Regarding the five aggregates, such as form and so forth:

that which has not yet arisen does not exist, and that which has already arisen must cease; therefore, they are truly impermanent. One should thus give rise to the understanding of impermanence in accordance with reality.

Because it is suffering at the time of suffering, because it is suffering when pleasure ceases, and because it is suffering throughout the three times of equanimity, it is in truth suffering; thus, one develops the understanding of it as suffering therein.
With impermanence as its cause and impermanence as its fruit, it is established through the relationship of cause and effect; because it depends on other attachments, the fruit is not autonomous.
The cause is likewise: that which has not yet existed comes into being, and that which has already existed returns to non-existence.
Since this occurs by virtue of prior causes, that which is dependent on others is also not autonomous.
Apart from cause and effect, there is no other distinct phenomenon that constitutes a self; therefore, non-self (*anātman*) is the reality, giving rise to the realization of non-self.
Impurity is of two kinds:
first, form; second, non-form.
There are three types of impurity regarding form, namely: initial, intermediate, and final.
"Initial" refers to the impurity of the seeds at the moment of conception when entering the womb.
"Intermediate" refers to the many impurities involved in the nourishment provided by food and drink after one has emerged from the womb.
The latter [type of impurity] refers to the state after one has cast off the body; it is impure because the physical form is destroyed and becomes various kinds of impurities.

As for that which is non-material (*arūpa*), it is non-material because it consists of states such as joy, sorrow, evil, the indeterminate, or the various fetters of non-detachment from desire; it is impure by virtue of these factors.
Therefore, the sage comprehensively observes that all three realms are impure.
Regarding these five aggregates as truly impure, he gives rise to the understanding of their impurity.
These four [realities] are all actual; therefore, they are not erroneous.
If one were to rely on the four virtues of the Buddha-nature, such as permanence and so forth, these four non-perversions would themselves become perversions;
it is to counteract these perversions that the four virtues of the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya are established.
The four virtues are: first, the perfection of permanence; second, the perfection of bliss; third, the perfection of self; and fourth, the perfection of purity.
As stated in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*: "World-Honored One!"

These sentient beings give rise to perverted thoughts regarding the five internal aggregates of clinging: they perceive the impermanent as permanent, suffering as happiness, the non-self as self, and the impure as pure.
"World-Honored One!

Because all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have never seen the realm of omniscient wisdom through their understanding of emptiness, they fail to cultivate the Tathāgata’s dharmakāya as it ought to be cultivated."

If a follower of the Mahāyāna, by virtue of faith in the World-Honored One, forms an understanding of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body as being permanent, blissful, self, and pure, such a person is not said to be inverted, but is said to have attained right view.
Why is this so? World-Honored One!
The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is the perfection of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
If a person holds such a view, it is called right view; such a person is a "son from the breast" (*uras-putra*) of the Tathāgata.
A "son from the breast" is so called because they always abide within the heart-mind of the Buddha.

Furthermore, regarding the four virtues and *pāramitās* of the Tathāgata, which proceed from cause through gradual deepening, one should know that when stated in reverse order, the latter becomes the former—namely: purity, self, bliss, and permanence.
Because icchantikas hate and turn their backs on the Mahāyāna, in order to overturn their delight in dwelling within the impurity of saṃsāra,
one should know that the cultivation of a bodhisattva’s faith and delight in the Mahāyāna dharma results in the attainment of the pure pāramitās as its fruit.

Because all non-Buddhists conceptually cling to the nature of the five aggregates, such as form and so forth, as being a self, yet these phenomena—form and the rest—are contrary to the characteristics of a self as you conceive it, they are eternally without a self.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, by means of the wisdom of suchness, attain the perfection of selflessness (*nairātmya-pāramitā*) regarding all phenomena; this is the perfection of selflessness.

Because it does not contradict the characteristic of selflessness as you perceive it, the Tathāgata says that this characteristic is eternally selfless. Since it is the true essence of all phenomena, he says that the perfection of selflessness is the self (*ātman*).
As stated in a verse of the sutra:
"The two emptinesses are already purified; One attains the supreme self of non-self.
Because the Buddha has attained the pure nature, Non-self is transformed into self."
Non-Buddhists and others cling to the view of a self within the five aggregates of grasping (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
To overturn this false attachment to a self, one practices the Prajñāpāramitā until the attainment of supreme non-self; it should be understood that this "self-pāramitā" is its fruit.

Because the śrāvakas fear the suffering and pleasure of saṃsāra and abide in the quiescent cessation of the suffering of saṃsāra, one cultivates the *ākāśaspharaṇa-samādhi* (space-pervading samādhi) in order to overturn this inclination toward [their] pleasure. It should be understood that the perfection of the pleasure of all marks—both mundane and supramundane phenomena—is its fruit.
Because Pratyekabuddha Āryas do not attend to matters such as the benefit of sentient beings, but instead delight in solitary dwelling in tranquility,

one should understand that the cultivation of a Bodhisattva’s great compassion for the sake of benefiting sentient beings— maintained and protected throughout the entirety of saṃsāra— is the result of the constant *pāramitās*.

Thus, these four causes—faith and delight in the Mahāyāna Prajñāpāramitā, the Ākāśagarbha-samādhi, and the great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) of a bodhisattva—are able to accomplish the four pāramitās of the Tathāgata’s dharmakāya. For this reason, the Buddha taught that by virtue of these four qualities, all Tathāgatas take only the dharmadhātu as supreme.
Just as space is taken as the limit and the ultimate finality,
what meaning is manifested by these four lines?

Because of cultivating faith and delight in the Mahāyāna, and because the Buddhas have attained the most supremely pure *pāramitās*, the Buddha taught that only the *dharmadhātu* is supreme and preeminent.
By practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, one attains the ultimate *nairātmya-pāramitā* regarding both the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*) and the world of the vessel (*bhājana-loka*).

The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are called the world of sentient beings and constitute the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*); the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the land are called the world of the vessel and constitute the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Because these two types of emptiness are what is revealed [by this practice], it is said to be "like space."

In order to cultivate the samādhi of the shattering of emptiness and so forth, one should attain mastery over all phenomena in all places according to one's will; therefore, space is taken as the ultimate limit.

Because of the cultivation of the Bodhisattva’s great compassion, one constantly gives rise to a heart of pity toward all sentient beings and protects them without limit; therefore, it is said to extend beyond the furthest limit of time.

Regarding "that which is beyond the limit of the future": even if there were a further limit to the future, the Great Compassion of the Bodhisattva would still be able to transcend it; therefore, it is established that both the noble and the ordinary stages prior to the [Bodhisattva] grounds do not attain the four virtues.

Furthermore, it should be understood that because the ten stages (daśabhūmi) are hindered by four obstacles, the four virtues of the ultimate fruit are not yet attained; it is only upon reaching the mind immediately following the diamond-like concentration (vajropamasamādhi) that they are finally acquired. Why is this so?
Beyond the three realms, there are three kinds of noble beings, namely: śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas of great power.

Within the untainted realm (anāsrava-dhātu), there are four kinds of hostile obstacles; because of these four hostile obstacles, one cannot attain the four kinds of perfection of merit (pāramitā) of the Tathāgata’s dharmakāya.

Regarding the four hostile obstructions: first, the birth-and-death of expedient means; second, the birth-and-death of causes and conditions; third, the birth-and-death of existence; and fourth, the birth-and-death of non-existence.

As for the first, the birth-and-death of expedient means, this is the ground of the dwelling of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*), which can produce new outflow-free karma (*anāsrava-karma*), just as ignorance produces volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).

If, through the means of afflictions (*kleśa*), a fruit of the same category is produced, it is termed a "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*), as when ignorance (*avidyā*) produces unwholesome formations (*akuśala-saṃskāra*).

If a fruit of a different category is produced, it is merely termed a "means" (*upāya*), as when ignorance produces wholesome formations (*kuśala-saṃskāra*) or immovable formations (*āniñjya-saṃskāra*).

Now, the production of new uncontaminated karma (*anāsrava-karma*) by the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*) is likewise: it may produce that which is of the same category or that which is of a different category. Producing meritorious formations (*puṇya-saṃskāra*) is called "of the same category," because they share the same object as conventional reality;
producing formations of wisdom (*jñāna-saṃskāra*) is called "of a different category," because wisdom is true insight.
This is called the birth-and-death of expedient means (*upāya*).

As for the second, the birth-and-death of causal conditions (*nidāna*), it refers to the outflow-free karma (*anāsrava-karma*) produced by the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*); this karma is termed the birth-and-death of causal conditions.

For example, the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) produced by ignorance are karma; they produce only results of a similar kind and do not produce results of a dissimilar kind. Wholesome actions produce only pleasant results, while unwholesome actions invite only painful retribution. Therefore, this is called "birth and death through causes and conditions" (*hetupratyaya-jarāmaraṇa*).
Conventional birth and death is analogous to the stage of ordinary beings;
causal birth and death is analogous to those from the stage of *srotāpanna* upward, who merely exhaust their past karma and do not produce new karma.

Regarding the existence of birth and death within the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), ignorance as the dwelling-ground (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) serves as the condition and untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*) as the cause; the three types of noble ones (*ārya*) possess bodies born of mind (*manomaya-kāya*).
For example, conditioned by the four graspings and with tainted karma as the cause, there arises a body within the three realms.
"Existence-existence" (*bhavābhava*) refers to future birth-existence;
furthermore, another birth is called existence-existence.

As for those *anāgāmins* who attain parinirvāṇa during their second birth as "those who go upstream," they are called "possessing existence" (*bhava*) because one birth remains. Regarding the four types of "non-existence of birth and death":
these refer to the final mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) of the three noble ones; conditioned by these, they are beyond the possibility of being conceived as subject to falling back.
For example, birth is the condition for the faults of old age, death, and so forth.

Therefore, the ground of the dwelling of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) is the locus upon which all afflictions depend. Furthermore, although all afflictions are collectively termed "ignorance," this is because ignorance is the root of all delusions. Since this root has not yet been completely extinguished, and because they are permeated by the foul stench of the habitual tendencies of all afflictions, Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and even sovereign Bodhisattvas cannot attain the Great Purity Perfection (*mahā-śuddhi-pāramitā*) that is free from all defilement.

Furthermore, based on these conditions, because this subtle conceptualization of the ground of abiding ignorance continues to circulate without ceasing, one is utterly unable to attain the Great Self-Pāramitā that is without activity and without ideation.

Therefore, with the ground of the dwelling of ignorance as the condition and the outflow-free karma arising from subtle conceptualization as the cause, because the three kinds of mind-made bodies arise, one cannot attain the Great Bliss Pāramitā that is utterly free from the suffering of cause and effect.

If one has not yet realized the Tathāgata’s nectar-like realm (*amṛtadhātu*), which is difficult to produce and difficult to exhaust through karma such that nothing remains; and if one has not yet realized the inconceivable realm free from falling back, because these have not been extinguished and have passed away, one cannot attain the ultimate, undifferentiated perfection (*pāramitā*) of old age, death, and so forth, which are eternally constant.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the ground of the dwelling of ignorance is like the difficulty of afflictions; uncontaminated karma is like the difficulty of karma; the three types of mind-made bodies are like the difficulty of karmic fruition; and inconceivable retrogression is like the difficulty of faults.
If one were within the three types of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*), there would be no perfections of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

Therefore, the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata possesses the four perfections of permanence and so forth: because all afflictions and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have been utterly extinguished in the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata, it is called "supremely pure" (*viśuddha*);
because all false attachments to self and non-self have ceased and subsided, it is called the "Great Self" (*mahātman*).
Because the causes and effects of the mind-born body have reached ultimate exhaustion, it is called Great Bliss;
because one has attained equal penetration into both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, it is called Great Permanence.
Furthermore, it should be understood that each of the four virtues has two aspects of conditions.
Regarding the first, because there are two causal conditions, it is said that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body possesses the Great Pāramitā of Purity:
first, intrinsic purity is termed the universal characteristic; second, stainless purity is termed the specific characteristic.
Because intrinsic purity exists throughout both the holy and the ordinary, it is called "universal" (tong).
Because stainless purity exists only in the fruit of Buddhahood, it is called "distinctive" (bie).
Furthermore, there are two kinds of causes and conditions for which the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is said to possess the *pāramitā* of the Great Self (*mahātman*).
